summary: Specifies how a server should behave to serve WebNFS clients. It is the server-side companion to the WebNFS client specification and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2055 describes server behavior for WebNFS clients. A client can start with a public filehandle and ask the server to look up several path components in one request, while the server still enforces its export rules.

questions: how does a webnfs server work
what is the webnfs public filehandle
subtitle: Server behavior for NFS clients that use a public filehandle and multi-component lookup.

tldr.problem: An NFS client normally uses portmap to find a server port and MOUNT to obtain an initial filehandle before looking up files.
tldr.mechanism: WebNFS servers accept a version-specific public filehandle and can evaluate a path with several components in one LOOKUP request.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo specifies server behavior for those extensions, including path handling and export access checks.

today: RFC 2055 is an Informational memo published in October 1996, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies server behavior for WebNFS extensions to NFS versions 2 and 3.

sections.title: Purpose of the Server Specification
sections.content:
WebNFS extends NFS versions 2 and 3 with server features intended to support conventional or web-browser clients. The extensions let a client obtain an initial filehandle without using the portmap or MOUNT protocols and let it request a path with multiple components.

RFC 2055 specifies what a WebNFS server supports to interoperate with clients. The companion client specification is RFC 2054. This memo also describes transport, path, symbolic-link and exported-filesystem behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: WebNFS adds ways for a client to begin an NFS lookup and request a path with fewer steps. This memo explains how the server responds to those requests.

sections.title: Transport and the Well-Known Port
sections.content:
The memo says WebNFS clients first try a TCP connection and try UDP if the server refuses it. Servers must support UDP and should support TCP. The RFC describes TCP as useful on wide-area networks because of its congestion control and error handling.

A WebNFS server must register on UDP port 2049, and on TCP port 2049 if it supports TCP. It must not reject WebNFS requests because they originate from a non-reserved port; clients are not required to use port numbers below 1024.
sections.plainLanguage: WebNFS clients try TCP first and can fall back to UDP. Servers use port 2049 and must not require the client to use a reserved source port.

sections.title: The Public Filehandle
sections.content:
A WebNFS client can use a reserved public filehandle as its initial filehandle instead of obtaining one through MOUNT. The memo defines the value differently for the two NFS versions because their filehandle formats differ.

For NFS version 2, the public filehandle contains 32 zero octets. For NFS version 3, it has zero length. The server associates this starting filehandle with a file or directory chosen by its administrator, subject to the server's export rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The public filehandle gives a client a defined starting point for a lookup. Its representation is 32 zero octets in NFS version 2 and a zero-length value in version 3.

sections.title: Multi-Component Path Lookup
sections.content:
A standard NFS LOOKUP request looks up one directory member. A client walking a path such as a/b/c therefore sends a separate request for each component, using each returned filehandle for the next request. WebNFS permits a LOOKUP relative to the public filehandle to include multiple path components; the server evaluates them and returns a filehandle for the final component.

A path beginning with a printable ASCII character uses canonical syntax: slash-separated components with percent escapes for specified characters. A path beginning with byte 0x80 uses the server's native path syntax. The memo also specifies how the server handles symbolic links during lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask the server to look up an entire path in one request. The client can use the defined slash-separated form or, when marked, the server's native path form.

sections.title: Export Boundaries and Security
sections.content:
If a path reaches a file outside the server's exported filesystems, the server must return an error. A server that relies on MOUNT for access checks cannot use a WebNFS lookup to grant access across exports, because WebNFS clients do not normally use MOUNT. A server that checks access on each NFS request can return a filehandle for a path spanning exports, since it can check later use.

The memo says the RPC security considerations for NFS versions 2 and 3 apply. Client and server may separately negotiate secure connection schemes for authentication, data integrity and privacy. It specifically asks implementors to consider the implications of paths that span exports.
sections.plainLanguage: A public filehandle does not remove the server's export restrictions. Servers must make sure that a returned filehandle cannot give unauthorized access across filesystems.
